name: Two-person dialogue: triangle system shot/reverse-shot
summary: Draw the line of interest through both actors' eyes and keep every camera on one side of it. Cameras sit on a triangle: the apex gives the two-shot master; external reverses (over-the-shoulder) and internal reverses (clean singles) are mirrored pairs at matched size, lens and height; parallel positions give profile singles. Matched pairs code equality; deliberately mismatched pairs code power. Change size or angle by at least 30 degrees between consecutive shots of the same subject.

editing: cut on line or reaction
L-cuts and J-cuts
progress from OTS to clean singles as intimacy or conflict rises
return to master to reset geography

rules.then: all cameras stay on one side of the line through the two actors' eyes (side A)
rules.why: keeps screen direction and eyelines consistent: A always looks screen-right, B screen-left

rules.when: consecutive shots of the same actor
rules.then: change angle by at least 30 degrees or change size by at least one step
rules.why: smaller changes read as a jump cut

rules.then: match size, lens and height across the reverse pair
rules.why: symmetrical coverage codes equality

rules.then: tighten or lower the dominant actor's reverse and widen or raise the weaker one's; or move from OTS (dirty) to clean singles as they emotionally separate
rules.why: breaking symmetry tells the audience the balance has changed

rules.then: cross via an on-axis neutral shot, a visible camera move across the line, or an actor move that redefines it
rules.why: an unmotivated crossing flips screen direction and disorients

avoid.what: mixing side-A and side-B setups
avoid.why: eyelines flip; the audience loses who is talking to whom

avoid.what: OTS shots where the foreground shoulder covers more than about a third of frame
avoid.why: crowds the speaker and hides the face

avoid.what: cutting between two singles of the same actor that differ by less than 30 degrees and less than one size
avoid.why: it reads as a jump cut, not a new angle

name: Master and coverage
summary: The safest, most editor-friendly way to shoot any scene: run the whole scene in a wide master that shows everyone and the geography, then repeat it in progressively tighter setups (two-shots, over-the-shoulders, singles), then pick up inserts and cutaways. Every setup respects the same axis of action, and every principal gets matched singles at the sizes the scene will need. The editor can then build rhythm and emphasis in the cut, returning to the master whenever geography changes or the audience needs to breathe.

editing: open on the master
move in as the scene intensifies
return to the master when blocking changes
inserts and cutaways as rhythm and cover
sound: consistent overlapping-free takes so lines cut

rules.then: all setups stay on the same side of the axis of action established in the master
rules.why: keeps screen direction and eyelines consistent so any setup cuts to any other

rules.when: cutting between two shots of the same subject
rules.then: change angle by at least 30 degrees or size by at least one step
rules.why: smaller changes read as a jump cut

rules.when: an actor moves to a new position in the master
rules.then: re-establish with the master (or a new wide) before cutting to coverage at the new position
rules.why: the audience needs to see the new geography or eyelines will seem wrong

rules.then: shoot wide to tight and match singles in lens and height for every principal
rules.why: lighting and continuity are set once for the wide; matched singles give the editor freedom to balance the scene

name: Walk-and-talk
era: Steadicam era (1976-present); TV codified in the 1990s-2000s
summary: Two (or more) characters talk while moving, and the camera moves with them so the scene gains energy, shows the world, and never stops for coverage. The core setup is a Steadicam or gimbal leading the pair, walking backward in front of them in a two-shot. Add a matched pair of leading singles or OTS shots, a lateral profile track alongside, and a following shot from behind for exits and reveals. Extras crossing the frame and the route itself (turns, doors, stairs) give the edit natural cut points and the scene a sense of purpose.

editing: long takes
cut at doors, turns and handoffs
cut on a step so the pace matches
a third character can join or peel off mid-shot

rules.when: the pair walks side by side
rules.then: keep the line through the two walkers and their direction of travel consistent; cover from in front (leading) and keep the same screen order of A and B in every setup
rules.why: if A is screen-left in one shot and screen-right in the next, the audience feels the pair swapped places

rules.then: match the walking pace and cut on a step or at a turn, door or handoff
rules.why: the route supplies motivated cut points and the matching cadence hides the cut

rules.then: let the pair stop and play the key line in a static two-shot or singles
rules.why: stopping after constant motion is itself emphasis; the audience leans in

recipes.why: The leading two-shot carries most of the scene in one take so performance and pace stay alive; matched leading singles give the editor emphasis without breaking stride, the stop lands the key line, and the follow shot hands the scene to the next location.

avoid.what: covering a walk-and-talk in static setups at stops along the route
avoid.why: the energy and the sense of purpose disappear; the scene becomes a series of standing conversations

avoid.what: long lenses on the leading shot
avoid.why: operating is shaky and the pair's distance to camera shifts focus constantly; 24-40mm keeps them stable and the world visible

avoid.what: the pair swapping screen sides between setups
avoid.why: breaks the walkers' axis and the audience feels a jump

name: Table scene (booth, dinner table)
summary: A table puts two to four people in a fixed circle where every pair has its own axis of action. Pick the dominant axis for the conversation that matters, cover that pair with matched reverses at seated height, and treat the others as reactions shot from the same side of that line. When the conversation moves to a different pair, re-establish: a wider shot or an overhead 'neutral' that shows the whole table resets the geography before a new axis takes over. A booth simplifies it to two facing pairs; a round table needs the most care.

editing: one dominant axis per conversation
overhead or wide reset when the axis shifts
reactions from listeners on the same side of the active line
inserts of food, glasses, hands as rhythm
sound: cutlery and room ambience as continuity

rules.when: a conversation between two people at the table
rules.then: choose that pair's line of action and keep every setup for that exchange on one side of it
rules.why: with several people at a table there are several lines; picking one per exchange keeps eyelines readable

rules.when: the conversation shifts to a different pair
rules.then: re-establish with a wide or an overhead neutral of the whole table before cutting to the new pair's reverses
rules.why: the overhead has no screen direction, so it resets the audience before a new axis takes over

rules.then: keep cameras at seated eye height and match the reverses in size and lens
rules.why: a standing-height camera looks down on everyone and unintentionally diminishes them

rules.when: cutting between two shots of the same diner
rules.then: change angle by at least 30 degrees or size by at least one step
rules.why: smaller changes read as a jump cut

name: Car interior
era: rear projection (1930s-60s), process trailer and car mounts, LED volume (2019-present)
summary: Two people side by side facing the same way, inside a box the camera cannot enter freely. The standard kit: a hood-mount two-shot through the windshield (the master), side-window singles from outside each door or a three-quarter single from the opposite seat, a back-seat POV/OTS that shows the road ahead, inserts of hands on the wheel and mirrors, and exterior tracking shots for geography and speed. Keep the driver on the same screen side in every frame, motivate light from the windows, and remember the road outside is the background of every shot.

color: day: bright exterior, contrast held by fill
night: dashboard glow, passing streetlight sweeps
editing: windshield two-shot as the master
singles from the side windows for emphasis
exterior tracking to reset geography and speed
inserts as rhythm
sound: road and engine hum as room tone
turn signal and wipers as rhythm

rules.then: keep the driver on the same screen side in every interior setup (driver screen-left through the windshield means passenger screen-right) and do not mix windshield and back-seat setups without a cutaway
rules.why: front and back views flip left and right; the audience will feel the occupants swapped seats

rules.then: match the background direction of travel in every setup and cut to an exterior tracking shot when the route or speed changes
rules.why: backgrounds moving in contradictory directions break the illusion of a single journey

rules.then: match the two singles in size and lens even though the camera positions differ (door mount vs opposite seat)
rules.why: equal framing keeps the two equal; a looser single on one will read as diminishing them

name: Single-character scene
summary: With no dialogue partner there is no shot/reverse, so the coverage has to come from the character's relationship to the space and to objects. Establish the environment, then cover the actor at varied sizes and angles (each change at least 30 degrees or one size step), and replace the missing reverse with what they look at: POVs, inserts of hands and props, details of the room. Action defines the axis here: the line runs along their eyeline or direction of movement, and the POV must match the eyeline that precedes it. Cut on action and on looks, and let a few shots hold long.

editing: cut on action
look then POV (eyeline match)
inserts compress process time
one long hold as the anchor
sound: room tone and action sound carry the scene
practical sounds (kettle, keys, phone) as punctuation

rules.then: cut to a POV or insert that matches the eyeline direction and height, then back to the character
rules.why: the look-object-reaction triad (eyeline match) replaces the missing reverse shot and tells the audience what they are thinking

rules.when: cutting between two shots of the actor
rules.then: change angle by at least 30 degrees or size by at least one step
rules.why: with only one person on screen every jump cut is exposed; the variation is what makes it read as coverage

rules.then: keep screen direction consistent across cuts (exiting frame right means entering the next frame from the left)
rules.why: the direction of movement is the axis of action in a solo scene

rules.then: compress it with a sequence of hand and prop inserts cut on action, anchored by one wider shot
rules.why: inserts carry the information and the rhythm while the wide keeps the audience oriented

name: Chase and escape (mount up and ride off)
summary: Movement scenes are covered for direction, speed and continuity of action. Establish where the movers start and where they are going, keep them travelling the same screen direction in every shot, cut on the action (a hand grabs, a leg swings, the next shot finishes the move), and sell speed with lens choice: a wide lens close to the subject makes the ground rush past, a long lens from far away stacks the background and shows effort. End on a wide that lets them leave the frame or shrink into the distance.

color: dust kicked up into the light
editing: cut on the action
constant screen direction
accelerate into the getaway, hold the final wide

rules.then: keep everyone travelling the same screen direction (left-to-right or right-to-left) in every shot
rules.why: a flip in screen direction reads as turning back or as a different chase; the audience loses who is going where

rules.when: a physical action spans two shots (grab, step, vault)
rules.then: start the action in the first shot and complete it in the second, cutting mid-movement
rules.why: the eye follows the motion across the cut, so the edit disappears and the action feels faster than either shot alone

rules.then: establish the start point and the destination direction in one wide before going close
rules.why: speed only reads against a known space; inserts without geography are just noise

rules.then: hold a wide while they leave frame or shrink to the horizon
rules.why: letting them go gives the escape its release and tells the audience they made it
